lessons.title: Mountains make their own weather
lessons.objective: You can estimate temperature change with elevation.

payload.prompt: It is 70°F at 4,000 ft. Roughly what at 10,000 ft?

explanation.correct: About right. Air cools roughly 3 to 5°F per 1,000 feet of elevation. At 6,000 ft higher, you are looking at 18 to 30°F cooler.
explanation.incorrect: Temperature drops 3 to 5°F per thousand feet of elevation. Do the math from the trailhead to your target.
explanation.sayThisLine: "It was 70 at the start, but probably 50 at the pass."

payload.prompt: Why does temperature drop as you climb?

options.text: Ground radiates heat; high altitude has less ground
options.explanation: The sun warms ground, which radiates heat upward. Higher up, less ground means less heating.

options.text: Air is thinner and holds less heat
The sun reflects off higher ground
You are closer to the cold sky

explanation.correct: The sun warms the ground, and the ground radiates that heat upward. Higher up, there is less ground doing that warming.
explanation.incorrect: The real reason: the sun heats the ground, and the ground warms the air above it through radiation. High altitude has less ground surface, so less heating.
explanation.sayThisLine: "The summit is cold because the sun heats the ground, not the air directly."

payload.prompt: Air cools per 1,000 feet of elevation.
payload.template: Air cools about {{rate}} degrees Fahrenheit per {{distance}} feet of elevation gain.

explanation.correct: This is the lapse rate: roughly 3 to 5 degrees F per 1,000 feet. Steep or moist air can vary a little, but 1,000 feet is the standard rule.
explanation.incorrect: The lapse rate is about 3 to 5 degrees F per 1,000 feet of elevation gain. Learn this rule and use it to estimate summit temperature from trailhead conditions.

payload.prompt: When reading a summit forecast, which should you use?

options.text: Town forecast below the mountain
Forecast for your summit's elevation
Average of town and summit forecasts
The highest temperature in the forecast range

explanation.correct: Always use the forecast for your elevation, not the town. The lapse rate means summit conditions differ from town conditions by dozens of degrees.
explanation.incorrect: Pick the elevation closest to your destination, not the town forecast. The summit forecast tells you what you will actually feel up there.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I checked the point forecast for the summit, not the town. Totally different."

statement.speaker: She
statement.text: Might rain at the summit. Will it be as cold as it feels?

payload.question: What is she asking?

options.text: Will rain make the summit feel colder than the forecast temperature?
options.explanation: Yes. She is thinking about wind and wet amplifying the cold.

options.text: Does temperature change with elevation?
Should I pack rain gear?

payload.translation: She understands that altitude and weather change together. Rain at altitude gets serious fast because wind chill adds to temperature drop.

followUps.line: It gets 3 to 5 degrees colder per thousand feet up, so yeah, the summit will feel it more. Rain at altitude gets serious fast.
followUps.why: You name the rule, then connect it to her situation. That is solid.

followUps.line: Should I bring a heavier layer?
followUps.why: They want your advice; follow up by asking about the elevation gain.

lessons.title: Point forecasts
lessons.objective: You can use a point forecast at the right elevation.

payload.prompt: What is a point forecast?

options.text: A forecast for an exact map location and elevation
A forecast for the nearest town
A forecast for the exact weekend you plan
A forecast of the best conditions in your area

explanation.correct: Right. A point forecast pins temperature, wind and rain to your actual destination on the map. Way more useful than town weather.
explanation.incorrect: A point forecast is location- and elevation-specific. You pick a spot on the map and get the forecast for there, not the town miles away.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I checked the point forecast for the pass, not the town. Totally different."

payload.prompt: What to read in a point forecast.
payload.template: A point forecast gives you temperature, wind speed, precipitation chance, and {{sky}} at the exact elevation you are heading to.

explanation.correct: Point forecasts include wind direction and gusts (crucial for mountains), cloud cover and whether you will see the summit. Read all of it, not just temperature.
explanation.incorrect: Point forecasts include wind direction, gusts, cloud cover and sky conditions. Each piece matters for your decision.

payload.prompt: A point forecast is most accurate for how long?

options.text: 3 to 6 hours; after that, precision degrades
The whole day; forecasts are accurate for 24 hours
Only 1 hour; mountain weather is too variable
Until dawn breaks and you see conditions yourself

explanation.correct: Weather forecasts get fuzzy beyond 6 hours. Mountains are especially touchy. Check it again the morning of the hike.
explanation.incorrect: Point forecasts are more precise than town forecasts, but they still degrade after a few hours. Plan as if you have maybe 3 to 6 hours of confidence, then trust your eyes.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I check the forecast the morning of, not three days out. Mountain weather moves."

statement.speaker: She
statement.text: The app says 50% chance of rain. Should we go?

payload.question: What is she asking?

options.text: Is 50% rain chance a reason to cancel?
options.explanation: She is really asking about the complete forecast, not just rain.

options.text: What matters more than rain chance at high elevations?
options.explanation: Wind speed and direction matter more than rain chance at exposed ridges.

options.text: Will it be cold enough to cancel?

payload.translation: She is reading the forecast but does not know which parts matter most for mountains. At elevation, wind is the decision-maker, not rain.

followUps.line: Fifty percent at the summit is worth checking the wind too. What is the wind speed and direction? That matters more than rain chance up high.
followUps.why: You asked for detail. Now you can actually decide.
You are prioritizing the real hazard: wind on exposed ground matters more than 50% rain.

payload.prompt: Do you hike or reschedule?

situation.narrative: You are planning a 6-hour ridge hike for Saturday. Thursday evening the point forecast shows: summit at 10,000 ft, 38°F, 35 mph winds with gusts to 50 mph, 20% rain, partly cloudy.

options.label: Cancel the hike. Wind that strong is dangerous on a ridge.
options.consequence: You wait for a calmer forecast and survive.
considerations: 50 mph gusts on a ridge at 10,000 ft with exposed terrain is serious. Wind chill and fatigue compound the risk.

options.label: Switch to a lower, more sheltered trail.
options.consequence: You still get a hike, but with reduced risk.
considerations: Lower elevation and sheltered terrain reduce wind exposure. Adapting the plan when risk rises is wisdom.

options.label: Start earlier Saturday to avoid afternoon wind.
options.consequence: Wind forecast likely holds all day; starting early does not solve it.
considerations: Wind does not follow a day cycle on ridges; it builds all day. Early starts help with afternoon thunderstorms, not wind.

options.label: Go as planned. Forecast might improve.
options.consequence: Fifty mph gusts are the real issue; gamble that conditions improve is unsafe.
considerations: Wind is not going to improve by Saturday. Never plan around hope that conditions will change for the better.

payload.expertNote: Forecasts degrade anyway; plan around what is predicted now. When risk rises, turn around or change the plan.

lessons.title: Afternoon storms, early starts
lessons.objective: You can explain why mountain hikers start early.

payload.prompt: What time should you start?

situation.narrative: You plan a 10-mile hike with 2,500 ft of gain to a ridge at 11,000 ft. Summer forecast: sunny morning, afternoon thunderstorms likely after 2 PM. You move at 2 mph on gentle terrain, 1 mph on steep. Expect 4 hours up, 2.5 hours down, 30 minutes rest. Sunset is 8:45 PM.

options.label: 5:30 AM (alpine start)
options.consequence: You summit around 1:00 PM, well before thunderstorms.
considerations: Alpine starts exist because mountains make their own weather. Afternoon storms are predictable; getting ahead saves lives.

options.label: 8:00 AM (normal early start)
options.consequence: You reach the summit around 3:30 PM, right into storms.
considerations: Being on exposed ridges when thunderstorms develop is the main lightning risk. Start early enough to clear summits by noon or 1 PM.

options.label: 10:30 AM
options.consequence: You summit around 5 PM, storms already built.
considerations: Afternoon storms in mountains are almost guaranteed in summer. Plan around them, not against them.

options.label: Start the night before and camp.
options.consequence: Unnecessary complexity for this hike.
considerations: Simple plans work best. An early morning start solves the problem simply.

payload.expertNote: Conservative timing on high peaks protects you from afternoon weather you cannot outrun.

payload.prompt: Put these steps in the right order for an alpine start:

items.text: Wake well before dawn (4 AM or earlier)
Load your pack the night before
Eat a full breakfast (you need fuel)
Wear more layers; it is cold at 4 AM
Hit the trail while stars are still out

explanation.correct: Proper order: pack was ready yesterday, wake early, fuel your body, dress warm (you will shed layers), start before dawn. An alpine start is simple once you plan the night before.
explanation.incorrect: Proper order: pack was ready yesterday, wake early, fuel your body, dress warm (you will shed layers), start before dawn. An alpine start is simple once you plan the night before.

payload.prompt: It is 6 AM on a sunny summer day at 9,000 ft, clear sky, light winds. You are making great time. Push for the summit?

scene.alt: A hiker at 9000 ft on a sunny morning with clear skies ahead.

choices.label: No, stick to the turnaround time

explanation.correct: Stick to the turnaround time you set at home. A beautiful morning is not a pass to ignore the plan. Storms can build fast at altitude.
explanation.incorrect: The whole point of alpine start is to get you off the ridge before storms build. Conditions now do not predict what happens in 3 hours. Honor the turnaround.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Perfect weather does not mean ignore the plan. Summits will be there tomorrow."

payload.prompt: Why do mountains build thunderstorms reliably in the afternoon?

options.text: Morning sun heats ground, creating rising air and instability
Afternoon air pressure drops
Afternoon wind shifts and collides with mountains
Jet streams shift in the afternoon

explanation.correct: Exactly. Sun heats the ground morning through midday, lifting air parcels higher and faster. By afternoon, cumulus clouds build into thunderstorms.
explanation.incorrect: Mountains amplify heating: more solar energy hits the ground, and terrain forces air upward. Afternoon is when lifting is strongest.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Storms build because of morning heat rising into the afternoon. It is the weather pattern in mountains."

statement.speaker: She
statement.text: Can we start at 9 instead of 6? I am not a morning person.

payload.question: What is she asking?

options.text: Can we do the hike with a later start?
options.explanation: Yes, but you need to explain the consequence.

options.text: Does the start time really matter that much?
options.explanation: She does not yet understand why mountain hikes require alpine starts in summer.

options.text: Is the hike too high for her?

payload.translation: She wants to hike but does not yet understand that summer mountain weather is predictable and dangerous. You need to explain why timing is critical.

followUps.line: Summer mountains build storms in the afternoon. If we start at 9, we could be on the exposed ridge when storms hit. An early start keeps us ahead of the weat...
followUps.why: You explained why the timing matters. Now she can make an informed decision.

followUps.line: Is there a lower trail option without the summit?
followUps.why: She listened and offered to adapt. That is good judgment.

lessons.title: Lightning on the trail
lessons.objective: You can name lightning precautions and when to make them.

payload.prompt: What is the right call?

situation.narrative: You are on a 10,000 ft ridge. You hear distant thunder maybe 5 miles away. Dark clouds are building on the horizon, but above you the sky is partly clear. You are 2 miles from the summit and 2.5 miles from tree shelter lower down.

options.label: Descend immediately to tree shelter.
options.consequence: You get off the lightning rod and reach safety.
considerations: Distant thunder means lightning is nearby. Ridges are lightning targets. Descend to lower, forested ground.

options.label: Stay, spread out the group, and wait.
options.consequence: You remain on the ridge in a developing storm.
considerations: A ridge in a developing storm is the worst place to hunker. Descend to lower, forested ground. Waiting on a ridge is unsafe.

options.label: Rush to the summit and back before the storm.
options.consequence: If you hear thunder now, lightning is within 15 miles.
considerations: There is no time to summit and descend safely. Descend and live.

options.label: Find a big rock to shelter under.
options.consequence: A large rock attracts lightning.
considerations: A large rock is a lightning target. Get low and move to lower terrain with trees.

payload.expertNote: When you hear thunder, lightning is within 15 miles. Get off ridges and into forest immediately. This is the safetyNote.

payload.prompt: You are caught in lightning in thick pine forest at 8,000 ft, trees all around of similar heights. Safe to wait it out?

scene.alt: A hiker in a dense pine forest surrounded by trees of similar height.

explanation.correct: Right. Dense forest of similar-height trees at lower elevation is one of the safer places to wait out lightning. Crouch on a pad if the ground is wet.
explanation.incorrect: Dense forest of similar-height trees is actually protective. The trees around you draw lightning more than you do. Crouch low, avoid touching trees.
explanation.sayThisLine: "If I get caught in a storm in the forest, crouch down, do not lean on trees."

payload.prompt: Caught in lightning on an exposed slab at 11,000 ft, trees 200 yards below. Safe to wait on the slab?

scene.alt: A hiker alone on an exposed rocky slab high on a mountain during a storm.

choices.label: No, descend to the trees immediately

explanation.correct: Descend to the forest fast. Exposed slabs with no surrounding trees are open to lightning. You are the tallest object on that slab.
explanation.incorrect: Open rock slabs are lightning targets. Descend to forest or lower ground, period. Descending in the lightning if the slab is worse is sometimes necessary.
explanation.sayThisLine: "If you are caught on a ridge, get lower and get to trees. Descend in the lightning if the slab is worse."

payload.prompt: Match each step to its reason:

pairs.term: Leave summits and ridges early when stor
pairs.definition: Ridges are lightning rods; get to lower, forested ground before cells hit

pairs.term: Spread out the group 50+ feet apart
pairs.definition: If lightning strikes one person, others can help; grouping increases total risk

pairs.term: Wait 30 minutes after the last thunder
pairs.definition: The storm is still producing lightning for at least 30 minutes after the last sound

pairs.term: Crouch low on an insulating pad
pairs.definition: Lower profile reduces strike risk; dry ground or pad reduces ground current

pairs.term: Avoid lone trees and rock formations
pairs.definition: Lone features draw lightning; shelter in dense forest or on ground surrounded by similar-height trees

explanation.summary: Lightning safety is about location (get off summits and ridges), isolation (spread out), timing (wait 30 minutes), and shelter (dense forest or low ground). None are 100% safe, but cut risk.

statement.speaker: She
statement.text: We got caught on the ridge when the storm hit. It was terrifying.

payload.question: What is she asking?

options.text: Did you descend to shelter, or hunker on the ridge?
options.explanation: That is the real question: what did you do and was it the right call?

options.text: Are you okay now?
options.explanation: That is empathy, but not engagement with what she learned.

options.text: Did you get struck by lightning?

payload.translation: She experienced a dangerous situation and is processing it. She needs to talk about the decision she made and whether it was right.

followUps.line: That is scary. What did you do? Did you get down to shelter, or did you have to hunker down on the ridge?
followUps.why: You asked what happened and recognized the two choices. That shows you understand the stakes.

followUps.line: We descended into the forest, which felt safer.
followUps.why: She made the right call. You should affirm it.

lessons.title: Wind, wet and hypothermia
lessons.objective: You can explain how wind and wet turn cool days dangerous.

payload.prompt: It is 45°F with 25 mph winds. What does it feel like?

explanation.correct: Around 33°F. Wind chill does not lower air temperature, but it steals heat from exposed skin fast. 25 mph wind at 45°F feels like freezing.
explanation.incorrect: Wind chill is the effective temperature your skin feels from wind evaporating moisture. At 45°F and 25 mph, skin feels near freezing.
explanation.sayThisLine: "It was 45 but with wind and rain I was shivering before I could get layers on."

payload.prompt: What do you do?

situation.narrative: It is 48°F, light rain has soaked you for an hour, you are breathing hard climbing at 8,000 ft. You have a shell jacket and are wearing a base layer and fleece. You are shivering noticeably and your fingers are going numb.

options.label: Stop, add a dry mid layer, eat and shelter from the wind.
options.consequence: You stop the heat loss and rewarm before it gets worse.
considerations: Shivering and numbness are early hypothermia signs. Get out of the wind, add insulation and food.

options.label: Hike faster to generate more body heat.
options.consequence: More sweat makes you wetter and colder.
considerations: You are already exerting; the problem is moisture, wind and wet clothes. Stop and rewarm before it worsens.

options.label: Descend as fast as possible without stopping.
options.consequence: Descending gets you to lower elevation but continued exertion worsens soaking.
considerations: Descending fast means more wind exposure and continued soaking. Stop, layer up first, then descend at normal pace.

options.label: Push on, it is only shivering.
options.consequence: Hypothermia progresses fast and decisions worsen.
considerations: Shivering means core temperature is dropping. It is the moment to act before judgment goes.

payload.expertNote: Hypothermia can kill in cool weather, not just cold. Wet + wind + exertion is the lethal combo. Stop and rewarm. This is the safetyNote.

payload.prompt: Which is a sign of hypothermia?

options.text: Confusion, slurred speech and poor decisions
Uncontrollable shivering
Fumbling, clumsy movements
Feeling warm and taking off clothes despite being cold

explanation.correct: All are signs of hypothermia at different stages. Early: shivering. Middle: fumbling, confusion. Late and dangerous: warm sensation and undressing despite freezing.
explanation.incorrect: Hypothermia has stages. Shivering comes first. Confusion and fumbling come next. Feeling warm and undressing is deep hypothermia and critical.
explanation.sayThisLine: "If someone stops shivering and says they feel warm, that is critical. That is deep hypothermia."

payload.prompt: It is 52°F and clear, but 35 mph winds are knocking you around on a ridge. You are dry but wind chill is near freezin...

scene.alt: A hiker on a windy ridge with strong gusts and clouds below.

choices.label: Yes, it is clear and dry

explanation.correct: Descend. Wind chill at 52°F + 35 mph means your skin feels like freezing. Exposure in that wind for hours risks hypothermia.
explanation.incorrect: Wind alone is enough. You do not need wet and cold. Wind chill + exertion + fatigue equals hypothermia risk even if you are dry.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Wind that strong on a ridge means getting down. Weather can change fast."

payload.prompt: Hypothermia can happen in cool weather.
payload.template: Hypothermia is dangerous cooling of the body core. It can happen in weather above {{temp}} degrees Fahrenheit when wind, wet and exertion combine.

explanation.correct: Hypothermia kills in temperatures well above freezing when you are wet and exposed to wind for hours. Classic scenario: cool, wet day with wind on a ridge.
explanation.incorrect: Hypothermia happens above freezing. The combination of cool temperature, wind and wet is deadly even at 50°F with exertion.

lessons.title: Heat forecasts
lessons.objective: You can read a heat risk rating and change a plan.

payload.prompt: What does a 'high' heat risk forecast mean?

options.text: Heat danger is elevated; outdoor activity should be limited
It will be a hot day, plan to bring extra water
It is a record-breaking temperature day
Only emergencies justify outdoor activity

explanation.correct: High heat risk means conditions are dangerous for outdoor activity. The forecast accounts for temperature, humidity and sun. Limit time and take breaks.
explanation.incorrect: A high heat risk is a danger rating for the public. It means reconsider outdoor plans or do them early/late with extreme caution.
explanation.sayThisLine: "High heat risk day? We are doing a dawn hike or skipping it."

payload.prompt: What is the wisest call?

situation.narrative: Saturday forecast: extreme heat risk. 98°F in the valley, humidity 45%, no clouds. You planned a canyon hike in a slot canyon (usually 10–15 degrees cooler). Water is limited; the seasonal spring might be dry.

options.label: Skip the hike until the heat wave passes.
options.consequence: You avoid real risk and can do the hike in safer conditions.
considerations: Extreme heat + slot canyon + uncertain water equals real risk. Wait a week.

options.label: Do a dawn start, turn around early, stay low elevation.
options.consequence: Short dawn hike at low elevation with plenty of water and rest can work.
considerations: Start before dawn, hike only until mid-morning, stay low, carry way more water than normal.

options.label: Do the slot canyon anyway; it is cooler there.
options.consequence: Do not bank on the canyon being cool enough. Heat illness is fast.
considerations: Slot canyons in heat waves are traps. Water is unreliable, emergency exit is slow, and heat still builds.

options.label: Carry tons of water and go anyway.
options.consequence: Carrying 5+ liters makes you move slower and hotter.
considerations: More water is good but does not solve extreme heat + unreliable springs + limited escape.

payload.expertNote: When the forecast shows extreme heat, skip outdoor plans or do a very short dawn hike at low elevation with abundant water. This is the safetyNote.

payload.prompt: On a 4-hour hike in high heat risk (normal in {{region}} is 2L), how much water?

explanation.correct: About 4 liters for 4 hours in high heat. Double your normal hydration rate. Heat dramatically increases water needs.
explanation.incorrect: Heat doubles or triples water needs. At high heat risk, plan for roughly 1 liter per hour or more if exerting hard.
explanation.sayThisLine: "High heat days? I carry twice the water and go half the distance."

payload.prompt: You are on a hot climb, drinking steadily, dizzy and nauseous, skin hot and dry. Heat illness or dehydration?

scene.alt: A hiker sitting down on a hot climb, appearing fatigued.

explanation.correct: Heat illness. You are drinking water, so it is not simple dehydration. Dizziness, nausea, hot dry skin mean your body is losing the battle against heat.
explanation.incorrect: Drinking water does not prevent heat illness in extreme conditions. Heat illness is core temperature rising dangerously. Descend, cool, rest and seek help.
explanation.sayThisLine: "If someone is dizzy and nauseous even after drinking, and their skin is hot and dry, get them down and cool them off."

statement.speaker: She
statement.text: The forecast says it will be hot but I still want to hike Saturday.

payload.question: What is she asking?

options.text: Can we hike anyway despite the heat risk?
options.explanation: Yes. She is asking if the forecast should stop you.

options.text: Is hot weather a problem for hiking?
Should we do a shorter hike instead?

payload.translation: She wants to commit to Saturday and is checking if you will say no. You need to offer alternatives, not just say 'no'.

followUps.line: Extreme heat risk days are not great for hiking. Could we do a dawn hike before it heats up, or pick Sunday when it cools?
followUps.why: You offered a solid reason and an alternative. She can make a real decision.

followUps.line: Good point. How about Sunday? The heat breaks then.
followUps.why: She accepted the reasoning and found a solution. You worked together.

lessons.title: Flash flood logic
lessons.objective: You can explain why rain miles away can flood a canyon.

payload.prompt: Is it safe to enter the slot?

situation.narrative: You are about to enter a narrow slot canyon for a 3-hour hike. The sky above is clear and sunny. The forecast mentions scattered thunderstorms in the mountains 20 miles upstream (out of sight). The slot is a narrow drainage with no escape.

facts.label: Drainage
facts.value: Funnels all upstream water to you

options.label: Skip it. Thunderstorms upstream mean flood risk.
options.consequence: You avoid the flash flood death trap.
considerations: Slot canyons are flash flood death traps. Rain miles away in the drainage feeds a flood down this channel.

options.label: Hike part way but stay ready to exit.
options.consequence: A flash flood moves too fast to react.
considerations: Once you are in, you are committed. By the time you see dark sky, water is minutes away.

options.label: Do the hike but establish a turnaround time.
options.consequence: A turnaround time does not protect you from water behind you.
considerations: Slot canyons in any rain risk are not negotiable. A turnaround does not protect you from water coming from behind.

options.label: Check radar before entering.
options.consequence: Even with radar, slot canyons are too dangerous.
considerations: Slot canyons and narrow drainages: if rain is forecast upstream or nearby, do not enter. Simple rule, it saves lives.

payload.expertNote: Flash floods in slot canyons are the leading cause of hiking deaths in canyon country. Never enter if there is any storm risk upstream. This is the safetyNote.

payload.prompt: It is sunny and 80°F where you are. Five miles upstream in mountains, a thunderstorm is dumping rain. Flood risk?

scene.alt: A sunny canyon bottom with mountains visible upstream where storm clouds gather.

explanation.correct: Absolutely. Water from that storm flows downstream toward you, channeled by the drainage. Sunny weather above you means nothing. Get to high ground.
explanation.incorrect: Canyons and washes channel water from upstream. Rain 5 miles away reaches you if you are in the drainage. Sunny at your location does not protect you.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Rain upstream is your problem, not rain above you. Get out of the drainage if there is a thunderstorm anywhere nearby."

payload.prompt: Heavy rain 10 miles upstream of your canyon. Where does that water go?

options.text: Flows downhill into drainages, all funneling toward your canyon
Most soaks into the ground
Stays in the mountains and does not reach lower canyons
The canyon wall blocks it from reaching the bottom

explanation.correct: All water flows downhill into drainage systems. Rain 10 miles upstream runs downhill into creeks feeding your canyon. It all converges into a flash flood.
explanation.incorrect: A canyon is a drainage. Water from anywhere in that watershed runs into it. All upstream rain reaches downstream canyons.
explanation.sayThisLine: "A canyon collects water from the whole area above it. Rain miles away becomes a wall of water down there."

payload.prompt: Why canyons are dangerous in rain.
payload.template: A flash flood is a sudden rise in water from rain miles away. In a narrow canyon, water has nowhere to go but {{path}} and can move as fast as a car.

explanation.correct: Flash floods in canyons rush downhill at high speed. The water is confined. There is no escaping by going sideways or climbing the walls.
explanation.incorrect: A canyon is a funnel for water. It has only two directions: down or backed up. Sideways and up are not options.

statement.speaker: She
statement.text: There is a forecast of scattered storms but we should be fine in the slot. It is narrow but we will move fast.

payload.question: What is she assuming?

options.text: That fast movement protects you from flash floods?
options.explanation: Yes. She does not understand that a flash flood moves faster than humans.

options.text: That the narrow slot is an advantage?
options.explanation: The narrow slot is actually the danger: water is confined and moves fast.

options.text: That scattered storms are low risk?

payload.translation: She does not understand that slot canyons funnel water and that you cannot outrun a flash flood. You need to explain the real risk.

followUps.line: Slot canyons are actually the riskiest place to be in a thunderstorm. Flash floods funnel through them, and there is no escape. If storms are forecast, we sh...
followUps.why: You explained the real risk clearly and offered an alternative. That is important.

followUps.line: I did not think about that. Let us do the ridge hike instead.
followUps.why: She heard the explanation and agreed. You worked it out together.

lessons.title: Smoke and fire weather
lessons.objective: You can read AQI and red flag warnings for a hike.

payload.prompt: An AQI of 150 means what?

options.text: Unhealthy for general public; limit outdoor activity
Good air quality, safe to hike
Moderate; some sensitive groups limit outdoor time
Unhealthy for sensitive groups only; most people are fine

explanation.correct: AQI 150 is unhealthy. At that level, wildfire smoke is thick, and outdoor exertion worsens respiratory stress. Limit time outdoors.
explanation.incorrect: The AQI scale: 0–50 good, 51–100 moderate, 101–150 unhealthy for sensitive, 151–200 unhealthy, 201–300 very unhealthy, 301+ hazardous.
explanation.sayThisLine: "AQI over 150? Smoke is heavy. We are doing a short, easy trail or not hiking."

payload.prompt: Should you do this hike?

situation.narrative: AQI in your area is 175 from wildfire smoke. A 6-mile mostly flat hike with 500 ft of gain is planned. You have no respiratory conditions. Water and shade exist on the trail.

options.label: Skip it; AQI 175 is unhealthy for exertion.
options.consequence: You avoid respiratory stress from hard breathing in thick smoke.
considerations: AQI 175 is unhealthy for outdoor exertion. Your breathing effort pulls more smoke into your lungs while hiking.

options.label: Do a much shorter, easier hike (2 miles, flat).
options.consequence: Very short hike minimizes exertion and smoke inhalation.
considerations: Flat, low-exertion hiking in high AQI is less stressful. Still not ideal, but limits damage.

options.label: Go as planned. You are healthy.
options.consequence: AQI 175 is unhealthy even for healthy people during exertion.
considerations: Climbing with heavy breathing in that smoke is asking for respiratory problems. AQI categories apply to everyone.

options.label: Wear a respirator mask and go.
options.consequence: Masks help but do not fully protect during hard exertion.
considerations: Even with a mask, hard hiking in AQI 175 stresses your respiratory system. Better to skip or do very easy walking.

payload.expertNote: High AQI + hiking exertion equals worsening respiratory stress. This is not about toughness, it is about not damaging your lungs. This is the safetyNote.

payload.prompt: Match each alert to its meaning:

pairs.definition: Wildfire smoke or pollution has made air unhealthy. Reduce outdoor exertion.
Fire weather alert: warm, dry, windy conditions when fires spread fast. No campfires, high fire danger.
A specific trail or area is closed due to wildfire or fire danger. Do not enter.
Smoke present but not at 'unhealthy' levels yet. Sensitive groups should limit outdoor time.

explanation.summary: Wildfire alerts come in layers: air quality, fire weather conditions, and trail closures. Read all three to know if your hike is safe.

payload.prompt: Red flag warning for your area. Can you have a campfire?

scene.alt: A campsite during a red flag warning with dry conditions and wind.

choices.label: No, do not have a campfire

explanation.correct: No campfire. A red flag warning means fire danger is extreme. Any spark becomes a disaster. Follow the alert.
explanation.incorrect: Red flag warnings are issued for a reason. Fire conditions are dry, hot and windy. Even 'careful' fires become dangerous fast.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Red flag warning? No fires, period. The whole forest is kindling."

statement.speaker: She
statement.text: The smoke rolled in today. AQI is like 200.

payload.question: What is she telling you?

options.text: She is saying air quality is bad and hiking is a bad idea?
options.explanation: Yes. AQI 200 is hazardous air. She is probably telling you she will not hike.

options.text: She is just complaining about the smoke?
She is asking if you should wear a mask?

payload.translation: She is telling you the air quality is bad (AQI 200 is hazardous) and that hiking plans should change.

followUps.line: That is hazardous air. Are you thinking of hiking this week? We might want to wait until it clears, or do something flat and super easy.
followUps.why: You read the alert and suggested concrete alternatives. She can make a decision.

followUps.line: Yeah, I was going to cancel. My lungs feel it.
followUps.why: You supported the right call. She is listening to her body and the conditions.

lessons.title: Snow and weather windows
lessons.objective: You can explain why lingering snow and short windows change trail plans.

payload.prompt: What should you plan?

situation.narrative: You want to hike a 9,000 ft pass in early July. SNOTEL shows snowpack at 140% of normal, much more snow lingering than average. The pass is normally snow-free by July 1.

options.label: Delay the trip to late July when clear.
options.consequence: You avoid snow hazards and enjoy clear tread.
considerations: Snowpack at 140% means the pass stays snowed in longer. Mid-July gives much better odds of clear tread.

options.label: Go as planned but bring microspikes and ice axe.
options.consequence: Equipment helps but does not solve the complexity.
considerations: High snowpack means postholing all day, hidden moats, unstable cornices. These are not just 'manage with gear'.

options.label: Pick a lower-elevation trail that is clear now.
options.consequence: Enjoy lower-elevation trails now and save the pass for later.
considerations: Adapting the plan when conditions are not right is wisdom, not failure.

options.label: Hope warm weather this week melts it fast.
options.consequence: Cannot count on one week of warmth.
considerations: Snowpack is based on months of accumulation. One hot week does not change 140% to clear.

payload.expertNote: Plan based on SNOTEL data, not hope. High snowpack lingers even in mid-July. This is the safetyNote.

payload.prompt: What is a weather window in hiking?

options.text: A gap in the forecast between storms when you can hike safely
A viewpoint along a trail
The season when a pass is normally hikeable
The time of day when sun hits the trail

explanation.correct: A weather window is a forecast gap where conditions are stable enough to hike safely. 'We got a weather window Sunday, so we went for it.'
explanation.incorrect: A weather window is a brief period of good conditions between storms or unstable weather. You take it fast because it is temporary.
explanation.sayThisLine: "We got a weather window Sunday, so we went for it. Monday it was storming again."

statement.speaker: She
statement.text: Can we do the pass next month? It will be snow-free by then, right?

payload.question: What is she asking?

options.text: When will the pass actually be snow-free?
options.explanation: Yes. She assumes a typical timeline but does not know about current snowpack.

options.text: Does she have enough snow skills?
Do you need special gear?

payload.translation: She wants to do the hike but is guessing at the timeline. You need to check the data and give her a real answer.

followUps.line: Depends on the snowpack. Let me check SNOTEL for that elevation. If it is high-normal or above, we might be postholing in June. We can wait or pick a lower t...
followUps.why: You explained why it matters and offered to check the data. That is partnership.

followUps.line: Oh, that makes sense. How do I read SNOTEL?
followUps.why: She wants to learn. You are teaching, not just deciding for her.

payload.prompt: What happens in spring snow.
payload.template: {{term}} is when you sink deeply into soft snow with each step, which slows you down and tires your legs fast.

explanation.correct: Postholing happens in corn snow (refrozen overnight melt) and deep spring snow. It is exhausting. Early season, you are postholing until melt consolidates the snow.
explanation.incorrect: Postholing is the technical term for sinking into soft snow. Early season snow travel is often postholing.

payload.prompt: Snowpack is 75% normal in March. Delay in clearance (normal: mid-June)?

explanation.correct: About 2 weeks later, so late June instead of mid-June. At 75% of normal, melt happens on a similar timeline.
explanation.incorrect: Low snowpack means melt happens roughly on time or slightly delayed. At 75%, it is closer to on-time or delayed about 2 weeks.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Seventy-five percent snowpack is still a lot of snow. Do not expect early clearance."
